--- title: "Introduction to Plotting in Python" error: true --- ## Goals 1. Understand the difference between **imperative** (`matplotlib`) and **declarative** (`seaborn`) plotting, and when to use each. 2. Practice plotting with three basic visualizations: the histogram, the boxplot, and the scatterplot. 3. Understand visualization as a tool for identifying structure. 4. Recognize forms in which Simpson's paradox can manifest. ## Overview ::: {#c06e1469 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns ``` ::: - `matplotlib` is a Python library for an **imperative programming** approach to plotting. + The user is responsible for instructing the computer *how to build a plot* using the library's primitives. + Highly flexible, but really verbose code. + `matplotlib` is a massive library. We typically only work with `matplotlib.pyplot`. + Canonical abbreviation: `plt`. - `seaborn` is built on `matplotlib` to support a **declarative programming** approach to plotting. + The user instructs the computer *what to build* using the library's primitives. + We don't see the details (initialize the `Figure` and `Axis`...), but lose some flexibility. + Canonical abbreviation: `sns`. For our purposes, `seaborn` is the most useful tool. Just keep in mind that `matplotlib` is the engine that makes the clean `seaborn` interface possible. We may need to create our own custom interfaces on data analysis projects. ## Dataset We'll continue to explore the Palmer Penguins data. Here we define a default style and fix the penguin colors to specific values. These colors should be friendly to different forms of colorblindness. ::: {#377f9f5f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = pd.read_csv(os.path.join("assets", "penguins.csv")) penguins = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g"]) # COLORS is a 'constant', so I prefer to use uppercase # to distinguish this variable name from others I might use # in a quick-prototyping context COLORS = {"Adelie": "#EA9839", "Chinstrap": "#984AE5", "Gentoo": "#469093"} sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") ``` ::: ## Basic Elements A `matplotlib` figure has two parts: - a **figure** (the canvas) and, - one or more **axes** (the panels with a coordinate system on them). The general workflow is: 1. Create both objects first. 2. Draw on individual axes as needed (often using a loop). 3. Add any annotations like axis labels, titles, or legends. Usually coupled with drawing on axes. The [`matplotlib` documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html) has an excellent quick start guide to help you become familiar with the basic elements. ::: {#e8112929 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # INITIALIZE: Lots of ways to do this. fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows = 1, ncols = 1, figsize=(6, 4)) # DRAW: Generally use NumPy arrays or Pandas Series/DataFrames as figure data. ax.scatter(penguins["flipper_length_mm"], penguins["body_mass_g"], alpha=0.6) # ANNOTATE: Provide the reader with helpful context ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)") ax.set_title("Heavier penguins have longer flippers") ax.annotate("alpha = 0.6", xy = (180, 6000)) # Nothing is displayed until you request it. plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=531 height=381} ::: ::: - `alpha=0.6` makes points partly transparent, so overlapping points are visible. - Label your axes with units (if relevant). Give your plots an informative title. - You can also add text annotations with `.annotate()`. Notice that the coordinates are based on the data values. ## Histograms A **histogram** partitions numeric data into *bins* and counts how many observations fall in each. This allows us to visualize the distribution of a single variable within our data. ::: {#46f41a34 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # INITIALIZE fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) # DRAW ax.hist(penguins["bill_length_mm"], bins=20, edgecolor="white") # ANNOTATE ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Count") ax.set_title("Distribution of bill length, all penguins") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=515 height=381} ::: ::: The number of bins is a choice, and it changes what you see: ::: {#38c68a29 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # INITIALIZE fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2), sharey=False) for ax, bins in zip(axes, [4, 20, 80]): # DRAW ax.hist(penguins["bill_length_mm"], bins=bins, edgecolor="white") # ANNOTATE ax.set_title(f"{bins} bins") ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") # This is helpful to eliminate extra padding/spacing at the end. fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1040 height=291} ::: ::: - **Too few bins**: Each bin captures a wide range so we miss small changes in the shape of the data's distribution. - **Too many bins**: Each bin tends to capture only a few values and gives the perception of highly complex distributional pattern. - Examine your assumptions as you calibrate the bins. + *Example*: Do we believe there are several distinct modes? Or only a few? + *Example*: Is the data symmetric? Or is it skewed in one direction? + How does your perception change your answers to these questions as you change the bin number? - You may need to experiment with a few values. + Make the computer work for you. Our basic `for` loop above lets us easily explore different values. + It's useful to write functions for specific plots so it works well in these kinds of loops. - Can also provide a `str` value to apply different heuristics in selecting the number of bins: + `fd`: [Freedman-Diaconis rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedman%E2%80%93Diaconis_rule). + `sturges`: [Sturges' rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturges%27s_rule). ### `seaborn` version Let's add the color variable. `seaborn` provides flexibility in how we specify a figure. - `data` keyword: Provide a source for information. - `x` keyword: Specify what information is mapped to the $x$-axis. - `hue` keyword: Specify what information is mapped to distinct colors. Needs *categorical data*. - Can also use arrays as in `matplotlib`. ::: {#104bf9af .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # INITIALIZE fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True) # FIGURE 1: All penguins sns.histplot(data = penguins, x = "bill_length_mm", bins = 25, ax = axes[0]) axes[0].set_title("All penguins") # FIGURE 2: Bill Length (mm) by Species sns.histplot(data = penguins, x = "bill_length_mm", hue = "species", hue_order = list(COLORS), palette = COLORS, bins = 25, multiple = "stack", ax = axes[1] ) axes[1].set_title("Colored by species") for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=1040 height=368} ::: ::: - **Left**: "Wide" distribution. Possible in principle, but the apparent peaks suggest additional structure. - **Right**: Each species has its own distribution with different centers and widths. - The stacked format is used for convenience here. Can hide information; e.g. how wide is the Adelie distribution? - How would you recover the picture on the right if you did not have the `species` labels? ## Boxplots A **boxplot** summarizes a variable's distribution with a few informative statistics. This is *potentially* richer than a table, and can be useful in comparing groups. Use this plot type only when it is actually more informative than the corresponding table! ![Siegel M (1999). The Joy of Mathematics; Parts 1 & 2.](assets/tukey1.png) General idea: - $x$-axis is used to convey information about categorical variable used to group numeric data. - $y$-axis conveys the numeric variable's information. - In principle, you can swap $x$ and $y$ axis. Use whatever is easiest to read. The **descriptive statistics** conveyed by a boxplot are - a measure of *location* or *center*, - a measure of *deviation* or *spread*, and - *skewness*, through the *symmetry/asymmetry of quartiles*. ### `seaborn` version ::: {#8ed320bc .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) sns.boxplot(data = penguins, x = "species", y = "body_mass_g", order = list(COLORS), # Ordered list specifying order along x-axis hue = "species", hue_order = list(COLORS), # Same idea as `order` palette = COLORS, legend = False, # This would be redundant. Set it to `True` to see why. ax = ax ) ax.set_xlabel("Species") ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)") ax.set_title("Body mass by species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=531 height=381} ::: ::: ### Reading a boxplot - The *line* inside the box is the **median**. - The *box* ranges from the **first quartile**, $Q_1$ (25% of the data lie below it), to the **third quartile**, $Q_3$ (75% lie below it). Each box represents the middle 50% of the data. Its height is the **interquartile range**, $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$. - The *whiskers* indicate a range of values that might not be considered "too extreme". + No farther than 1.5 times IQR below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. - Any *points* or *dots* outside the whiskers are flagged as **potential outliers**. We can compute the cutoffs ourselves for one species: ::: {#5eb09016 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} adelie = penguins.loc[penguins["species"] == "Adelie", "body_mass_g"] q1, q3 = adelie.quantile([0.25, 0.75]) iqr = q3 - q1 pd.Series( [q1, q3, iqr, q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr, adelie.min(), adelie.max()], index = ["Q1", "Q3", "IQR", "LB", "UB", "Min", "Max"] ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` Q1 3350.0 Q3 4000.0 IQR 650.0 LB 2375.0 UB 4975.0 Min 2850.0 Max 4775.0 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: No Adelie penguin has body mass outside the whisker range, so there are no points or dots shown for that box. ### Why do we use 1.5 IQR? The boxplot is the invention of American statistician [John Tukey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tukey). He was a vocal advocate for building visualization tools and is credited with the term "bit". ![](assets/tukey2.png) - There are various, well-informed heuristics for identifying outliers. Such rules do not prove a data point is in fact an outlier! - Tukey's 1.5 rule is somewhat arbitrary, but it is based on the following facts: + If data are approximately normal with mean $0$ and variance $1$, then $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{3}$ correspond to $-0.6745$ and $+0.6745$, respectively. + Thus, you can show that $\mathrm{IQR}$ is approximately equal to $2 \times 0.6745 \sigma$ for approximately normal data. + Any data points that is roughly $\pm 2.7$ standard deviations away from the mean gets flagged as a potential outlier. The points flagged by a boxplot should prompt you to examine those data points (e.g. look at the other variables' values). ### `matplotlib` version The imperative approach is quite verbose. It is worth seeing this once to appreciate the utility of the `seaborn` interface: ::: {#c4c03ef9 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) species_names = list(COLORS) # Create a list the contains data for each box data = [penguins.loc[penguins["species"] == s, "body_mass_g"] for s in species_names] # The list of arrays can be passed to `.boxplot()`. # What is `patch_artist`? This feature needs to be used so we can edit the display of the median line. parts = ax.boxplot(data, tick_labels = species_names, patch_artist = True, medianprops = dict(color = "black", linewidth = 2) ) # This is needed to set the colors of each box... How tedious! for patch, name in zip(parts["boxes"], species_names): patch.set_facecolor(COLORS[name]) patch.set_alpha(0.8) ax.set_xlabel("Species") ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)") ax.set_title("Body mass by species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=531 height=381} ::: ::: - Examine this figure and compare to the `seaborn` version. - What are defaults might `seaborn` have set for us? There is at least one visual element that is different. ## Scatterplots A **scatterplot** displays two numeric variables plotted against each other, one variable per axis. It useful for probing potential relationships, specifically associations, between variables. The `seaborn` interface allows you to fit linear trend lines to data. + This is done via *regression*, and it is not limited to linear trends. + We will review simple learning regression later in the course. + A *positive slope* indicates a **positive correlation**. Both variables "move together." + A *negative slope* indicates a **negative correlation**. The two variables "move in opposite directions." ### `matplotlib` version ::: {#d3542490 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = penguins["bill_length_mm"] y = penguins["bill_depth_mm"] # NumPy's `polyfit` can fit different trend lines slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, deg = 1) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) # DRAW: Scatterplot of data ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.6) # DRAW: Trend line xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 50) ax.plot(xs, intercept + slope * xs, color="red", linestyle="--") ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)") ax.set_title("All penguins together") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=515 height=381} ::: ::: ### `seaborn` version ::: {#e9b8f3c3 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) sns.regplot( data = penguins, x = "bill_length_mm", y = "bill_depth_mm", ci = None, # no confidence band; don't use this blindly! scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.6}, line_kws = {"color": "red", "linestyle": "--"}, ax = ax, ) ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)") ax.set_title("All penguins together") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=515 height=381} ::: ::: ## Simpson's paradox **Observation:** Across all penguins in our data, longer bills tend to go with *shallower* bills, as suggested by our scatterplots. Does this actually happen to individual penguins? Let us add the third variable we have been ignoring. ### `matplotlib` version We color each point by `species` and fit separate trend lines: ::: {#d673e5ec .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots() for species, color in COLORS.items(): sub = penguins[penguins["species"] == species] # DRAW: Scatterplot for particular species ax.scatter(sub["bill_length_mm"], sub["bill_depth_mm"], color = color, alpha = 0.7, label = species ) # DRAW: Species-specific trend line m, b = np.polyfit(sub["bill_length_mm"], sub["bill_depth_mm"], deg = 1) xs = np.linspace(sub["bill_length_mm"].min(), sub["bill_length_mm"].max(), 50) ax.plot(xs, b + m * xs, color=color, linewidth=2) ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)") ax.set_title("Penguin bill dimensions by species") ax.legend(title="Species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=589 height=455} ::: ::: ### `seaborn` version The `lmplot` function draws a scatterplot with a fitted line for each value of `hue`: ::: {#55164872 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # No initialization; this function creates its own canvas (`Figure` and `Axis`) by default. sns.lmplot(data = penguins, x = "bill_length_mm", y = "bill_depth_mm", hue = "species", hue_order = list(COLORS), palette = COLORS, ci = None, aspect = 1 ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=574 height=464} ::: ::: ### Why does this happen? The apparent trend reverses once we include group information! Each penguin species clearly shows a positive correlation between bill depth and bill length. The negative slope in the previous scatterplots came from combining three clusters that sit in different places. ::: {#4f02cc20 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]].mean().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` bill_length_mm 43.9 bill_depth_mm 17.2 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#64c63e63 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("species")[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]].mean().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm
species
Adelie 38.8 18.3
Chinstrap 48.8 18.4
Gentoo 47.5 15.0
``` ::: ::: The different species differ considerably in both variables. - Gentoo penguins have long, shallow bills - Adelie penguins have short, deep bills. Differences *between* the groups produced a downward trend when viewing the data without overlaying group structure The relationship *within* each group, however, clearly has a positive trend. This is an instance of **Simpson's paradox**, which is the phenomenon of reversing or eliminating trends within two variables once a third variable is included. - The third variable can be categorical or continuous. - Neither view is "wrong" as far as the mathematics are concerned. - The way to resolve the apparent paradox is to understand that a statistic, regardless of whether it is a single number of a trend, is inherently a summary *about a population*, not about individual observations. - What matters in practice is being clear about **which population you are interested in investigating**. Notice that not every relationship reverses. Body mass and flipper length rise together for all penguins *and* within each species, but the strength differs. ## Quick plotting with `pandas` `pandas` data frames have plotting implemented as a method. It is convenient for quick prototyping and exploratory analysis in a REPL. Each call returns a customizable axis object from `matplotlib`. ::: {#58e73e95 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = (penguins["body_mass_g"] .plot(kind = "hist", bins = 25, edgecolor = "white") ) ax.set_xlabel("Body mass (g)") ax.set_title("Body mass distribution for Palmer Penguins") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=589 height=455} ::: ::: A **scatter matrix** is useful if you want a quick look of several numeric variables at once. Keep in mind that this is a screening tool: - It merely suggests relationships and clusters worth a closer look. - It can be misleading, even if you factor in categorical variables, because it displays data in a pairwise fashion. ::: {#b1301f0b .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} numeric_cols = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"] pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(penguins[numeric_cols], c = penguins["species"].map(COLORS), # Color each point by its species diagonal = "hist", # Control the display along the diagonal alpha = 0.7, figsize = (8, 8), ) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=752 height=752} ::: ::: - Might need to adjust `figsize` to correctly display all visual elements. - With $p$ variables there are $p^2$ panels, so this is only viable for examining a few variables. ## Saving a figure ::: {#d53762c3 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create a directory to store our work; don't do anything if it already exists. os.makedirs("output", exist_ok = True) # Use the `.savefig()` method for a `Figure` object fig.savefig( os.path.join("output", "bill_scatter.png"), dpi = 200, # Dots per inch; resolution bbox_inches = "tight" # Control the bounding box ) ``` ::: ## Takeaway messages - Always plot grouped data if the structure is given to you. + Summaries and correlations over a mixture might not describe any of those groups. - It is difficult for humans to intuit latent structure from numeric summaries alone. Plots often provide a richer, high-level summary. - Apparent clusters in your visualizations are rarely an accident. + Ask what the groups might exist, and whether they might labeled somehow. + Use visualizations to help guide and sharpen your analysis. - Use `seaborn` for fast exploration and `matplotlib` when you need to control the details. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1: One variable 1. Make a histogram of `flipper_length_mm` with 30 bins. Describe its shape in one sentence. 2. Make the same histogram with `seaborn`, colored by species. Is this more or less informative? ### Exercise 2: Groups 1. Make a boxplot of `flipper_length_mm` by `island`. 2. Make a second boxplot of `flipper_length_mm` by `species`. Which grouping better separates the flipper lengths? Why might the island plot be misleading? ### Exercise 3: Associations 1. Make a scatterplot of `body_mass_g` ($y$-axis) against `flipper_length_mm` ($x$-axis), colored by species. Include a trend line for each species. 2. Does the overall relationship reverse within species, as the bill example did, or only change in strength? Justify your answer by computing correlations using `groupby` on the Pandas data frame. 3. Which of the three species shows the weakest association?
